street_items.meaning: Lafa (chewy Iraqi flatbread wrap)
street_items.streetShift: At every shawarma or falafel counter, the vendor's first question is 'פִּיתָה אוֹ לַאפָה?' (Pita or Lafa?). Lafa is larger, soft, rolled fresh on the spot, and holds generous portions of meat and salads without tearing.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Pita or lafa wrap?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: In a lafa, please!

exampleSentence.hebrew: שִׂים לִי בְּלַאפָה, עִם הַכֹּל וְהַרְבֵּה חָרִיף!
exampleSentence.spoken: Sim li b'lá-fa, im ha-kól ve-har-bé cha-ríf!
exampleSentence.english: Put it in a lafa for me, with everything and plenty of spicy!
exampleSentence.tts: שִׂים לִי בְּלַאפַה, עִם הַכֹּל וְהַרְבֵּה חָרִיף!

street_items.situationPrompt: You stand before the sizzling rotating shawarma spit. The carver raises his knife and asks: 'פִּיתָה אוֹ לַאפָה?'. You want the large, rolled flatbread wrap. What do you say?

street_items.meaning: Pita (fluffy Israeli pocket bread)
street_items.streetShift: Israeli pita is famously thick, pillowy, and steamy—designed to absorb tahini and hummus juices without leaking. It's the classic, lighter alternative to a giant lafa.

dialogue.lineHebrewA: בְּמָה לָשִׂים לְךָ, פִּיתָה אוֹ לַאפָה?
dialogue.lineSpokenA: Bema lasim lecha, pita o lafa?
dialogue.lineEnglishA: What should I put it in, pita or lafa?
dialogue.ttsA: בְּמָה לָשִׂים לְךָ, פִּיתָה אוֹ לַאפַה?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: In a pita pocket, thanks!

exampleSentence.hebrew: מָנָה פָלָאפֶל בְּפִיתָה, עִם הַרְבֵּה טְחִינָה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Maná faláfel b'pí-ta, im har-bé tchi-ná!
exampleSentence.english: A portion of falafel in a pita, with plenty of tahini!
exampleSentence.tts: מָנָה פָלָאפֶל בְּפִיתָה, עִם הַרְבֵּה טְחִינָה

street_items.situationPrompt: The falafel master points with his tongs: 'בְּמָה לָשִׂים לְךָ?'. You want the classic fluffy pocket bread. What do you reply?

street_items.meaning: With everything / the works (all salads & sauces)
street_items.streetShift: Never list individual salads one by one! In authentic street Hebrew, say 'עִם הַכֹּל!' (im hakol) to tell the vendor to load all the fresh salads, cabbage, pickles, hummus, and tahini.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: What salads should I put in for you?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: עִם הַכֹּל, וְשִׂים לִי הַרְבֵּה חָרִיף!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Im ha-kól, ve-sim li har-bé cha-ríf!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: With everything, and put lots of spicy for me!
dialogue.ttsB: עִם הַכֹּל, וְשִׂים לִי הַרְבֵּה חָרִיף

exampleSentence.hebrew: שִׂים לִי שַׁוַארְמָה עִם הַכֹּל, כָּל הַסָּלָטִים!
exampleSentence.spoken: Sim li shavarma im hakol, kol hasalatim!
exampleSentence.english: Make me shawarma with everything, all the salads!
exampleSentence.tts: שִׂים לִי שַׁוַארְמָה עִם הַכֹּל, כָּל הַסָּלָטִים

street_items.situationPrompt: You are at a crowded shawarma counter. The vendor holds the tongs ready over 8 salad trays and asks: 'מָה לָשִׂים לְךָ?'. You want the works—all salads, pickles, and tahini. What do you shout?

street_items.meaning: Plenty of spicy (schug / harissa hot sauce)
street_items.streetShift: Israeli street hot sauce (schug or harissa) packs serious heat. Asking for 'הרבה חריף' signals to the stall owner that you can handle real Yemenite/North African chili paste.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Put spicy sauce in your pita?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Yes bro, put plenty of spicy!

exampleSentence.hebrew: אֲנִי אוֹהֵב הַרְבֵּה חָרִיף עִם הַטְּחִינָה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Ani ohev harbe charif im hat'china!
exampleSentence.english: I love plenty of spicy with the tahini!
exampleSentence.tts: אֲנִי אוֹהֵב הַרְבֵּה חָרִיף עִם הַטְּחִינָה

street_items.situationPrompt: The vendor lifts a spoonful of fiery red and green schug: 'רוֹצֶה חָרִיף?'. You love strong chili heat. How do you instruct him?

street_items.meaning: Without amba (tangy Iraqi pickled mango sauce)
street_items.streetShift: Amba is a fragrant, bright yellow Iraqi fermented mango-fenugreek condiment. It has a potent smell and distinct flavor. If you don't want it, state 'בְּלִי עַמְבָּה' early before the vendor drizzles it.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Should I put amba sauce on top?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: No, without amba, only tahini!

exampleSentence.hebrew: בְּבַקָּשָׁה שִׂים לִי סַבִּיחַ, אֲבָל בְּלִי עַמְבָּה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Bevakasha sim li sabich, aval bli amba!
exampleSentence.english: Please make me a sabich, but without amba!
exampleSentence.tts: בְּבַקָּשָׁה שִׂים לִי סַבִּיחַ, אֲבָל בְּלִי עַם-בָּה!

street_items.situationPrompt: The sabich maker hovers a ladle of bright yellow pickled mango sauce over your pita and asks: 'לָשִׂים עַמְבָּה?'. You dislike fenugreek. How do you halt him?

street_items.meaning: Only tahini (no extras / sauces)
street_items.streetShift: Tahini is the sacred baseline of Israeli street food. If you want a mild, creamy sandwich without hot peppers or pickled mango, say 'רַק טְחִינָה'.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Which sauces should I put for you?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Only tahini, pour plenty on top!

exampleSentence.hebrew: בְּלִי חָרִיף וּבְלִי עַמְבָּה, רַק טְחִינָה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Bli charif uvli amba, rak tchina!
exampleSentence.english: No spicy and no amba, just tahini!
exampleSentence.tts: בְּלִי חָרִיף וּבְלִי עַם-בָּה, רַק טְחִינָה!

street_items.situationPrompt: The vendor asks: 'אֵיזֶה רְטָבִים?' (Which sauces?). You want pure sesame puree and zero hot peppers. What do you order?

street_items.meaning: For here / Dine in (literally: to sit)
street_items.streetShift: At every Israeli counter, café, or hummus joint, the first register question is 'לָשֶׁבֶת אוֹ לָקַחַת?' (To sit or to take?). If dining at the tables, reply 'לָשֶׁבֶת!'.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Hello, for here or to go?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: לָשֶׁבֶת, תּוֹדָה, תֵּן לִי צַלַּחַת מַסַבָּחָה!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: La-shé-vet, to-dá, ten li tzalachat masabacha!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: For here, thanks, give me a plate of warm masabacha!

exampleSentence.hebrew: אֲנַחְנוּ רוֹצִים לָשֶׁבֶת בַּחוּץ בַּשֶּׁמֶשׁ!
exampleSentence.spoken: Anachnu rotzim lashevet bachutz bashemesh!
exampleSentence.english: We want to sit outside in the sun!

street_items.situationPrompt: You arrive at Abu Hassan in Jaffa. The host asks at the door: 'לָשֶׁבֶת אוֹ לָקַחַת?'. You want a table inside. What is your response?

street_items.meaning: To take away / To go
street_items.streetShift: When you say 'לָקַחַת', the vendor wraps the sandwich tightly in foil and paper, bags it, and adds napkins and pickles on the side for your journey.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Is this to sit here or to go?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: To go, wrap it tight for the road!

exampleSentence.hebrew: שְׁתֵּי מָנוֹת פָלָאפֶל לָקַחַת, בְּבַקָּשָׁה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Shtei manot falafel lakachat, bevakasha!
exampleSentence.english: Two falafel servings to go, please!

street_items.situationPrompt: You are on your lunch break heading back to the office. The bakery cashier asks: 'לָשֶׁבֶת אוֹ לָקַחַת?'. What is your answer?

street_items.meaning: 'Enjoy your new thing!' (Traditional blessing on any new purchase)
street_items.streetShift: When an Israeli buys clothing, shoes, a phone, or gets a haircut, friends and shop owners always say 'תִּתְחַדֵּשׁ!' (male) or 'תִּתְחַדְּשִׁי!' (female). The standard reply is 'תּוֹדָה רַבָּה!'!

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Here is your shirt, enjoy your new item!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Thanks so much bro, awesome!

exampleSentence.hebrew: אֵיזֶה נַעֲלַיִם יָפוֹת, תִּתְחַדֵּשׁ!
exampleSentence.spoken: Eize na'alayim yafot, titchadesh!
exampleSentence.english: What nice shoes, enjoy them!

street_items.situationPrompt: You just bought a jacket at the market. The shopkeeper hands you the bag with a warm smile and says: 'תִּתְחַדֵּשׁ!'. What does he mean?
street_items.situationCorrect: Enjoy your new purchase! (Traditional congratulatory blessing)
situationDistractors: Hurry up and leave the shop!
Do you want to exchange this tomorrow?

street_items.meaning: Anything else?
street_items.streetShift: At every Israeli register before giving the total, the cashier asks 'עוֹד מַשֶּׁהוּ?' (anything else? a drink, gum, etc.).

dialogue.lineHebrewA: עוֹד מַשֶּׁהוּ, שְׁתִיָּה אוֹ מַשֶּׁהוּ מָתוֹק?
dialogue.lineSpokenA: Od mashehu, shtiya o mashehu matok?
dialogue.lineEnglishA: Anything else, a drink or something sweet?
dialogue.ttsA: עוֹד מַשֶּׁהוּ, שְׁתִיָּה אוֹ מַשֶּׁהוּ מָתוֹק?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: לֹא תּוֹדָה, זֶה הַכֹּל, אֶפְשָׁר חֶשְׁבּוֹן!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Lo toda, ze hakol, efshar cheshbon!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: No thanks, that's everything, can I pay!

exampleSentence.hebrew: עוֹד מַשֶּׁהוּ אָחִי, אוֹ שֶׁנִּסְגֹּר חֶשְׁבּוֹן?
exampleSentence.spoken: Od mashehu achi, o shenisgor cheshbon?
exampleSentence.english: Anything else bro, or shall we close the check?
exampleSentence.tts: עוֹד מַשֶּׁהוּ אָחִי, אוֹ שֶׁנִּסְגֹּר חֶשְׁבּוֹן?

street_items.situationPrompt: The cashier has rung up your borekas and asks: 'עוֹד מַשֶּׁהוּ?'. What is she inquiring about?
street_items.situationCorrect: Whether you'd like to add anything else to your order
situationDistractors: Whether you are paying by cash or credit card

street_items.meaning: That is all / that's everything
street_items.streetShift: When the cashier or vendor asks 'עוֹד מַשֶּׁהוּ?', the clean natural response is 'זֶה הַכֹּל!' (ze hakol). It signals you are ready for the final bill.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Anything else for you?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: That's all, give me the total!

exampleSentence.hebrew: רַק קָפֶה וּמַיִם, זֶה הַכֹּל!
exampleSentence.spoken: Rak kafe umayim, ze hakol!
exampleSentence.english: Just coffee and water, that's everything!

street_items.situationPrompt: The bakery clerk holds the tongs waiting to see if you want cookies too: 'עוֹד מַשֶּׁהוּ?'. You are finished ordering. How do you signal wrap-up?

street_items.meaning: Large cafe hafuch (Israeli latte / cappuccino)
street_items.streetShift: 'קפה הפוך' (literally 'upside-down coffee') is Israel's national espresso drink: steamed milk first, espresso poured over, topped with velvety foam. Saying 'הפוך גדול' is the most common morning sentence in Tel Aviv.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Good morning, what can I get you?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: הָפוּך גָּדוֹל בְּבַקָּשָׁה, עִם חֲלַב שִׁבּוֹלֶת!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Ha-fúch ga-dól bevakasha, im chalav shibolet!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: A large hafuch please, with oat milk!

exampleSentence.hebrew: אֲנִי חַיָּב הָפוּך גָּדוֹל כְּדֵי לְהִתְעוֹרֵר הַבֹּקֶר!
exampleSentence.spoken: Ani chayav hafuch gadol kedei lehit'orer haboker!
exampleSentence.english: I must have a large hafuch to wake up this morning!
exampleSentence.tts: אֲנִי חַיָּב הָפוּך גָּדוֹל כְּדֵי לְהִתְעוֹרֵר הַבֹּקֶר

street_items.situationPrompt: You walk into Aroma or a hip Tel Aviv cafe at 8:30 AM. The barista looks up: 'מָה תִּרְצֶה?'. You want Israel's signature large layered latte. What do you order?

street_items.meaning: Oat milk (short for חלב שיבולת שועל)
street_items.streetShift: Israel has the highest per-capita vegan population in the world, and oat milk is offered at 100% of coffee shops without question. Locals abbreviate 'חלב שיבולת שועל' to just 'חלב שיבולת'.

dialogue.lineHebrewA: עִם אֵיזֶה חָלָב לַעֲשׂוֹת לְךָ אֶת הַקָּפֶה?
dialogue.lineSpokenA: Im eize chalav la'asot lecha et hakafe?
dialogue.lineEnglishA: With what milk should I make your coffee?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: With oat milk, please!

exampleSentence.hebrew: קָפֶה קַר עִם חֲלַב שִׁבּוֹלֶת זֶה הֲכִי טָעִים בַּקַּיִץ!
exampleSentence.spoken: Kafe kar im chalav shibolet ze hachi taim bakayitz!
exampleSentence.english: Iced coffee with oat milk is the tastiest in summer!
exampleSentence.tts: קָפֶה קַר עִם חֲלַב שִׁבּוֹלֶת זֶה הֲכִי טָעִים

street_items.situationPrompt: You ordered a cappuccino and the barista asks: 'עִם אֵיזֶה חָלָב?' (Which milk?). You want oat milk. How do you specify?

street_items.meaning: Without sugar / Unsweetened
street_items.streetShift: If you don't mention sugar, Israeli baristas leave it unsweetened and point you to the sugar caddy on the counter. Saying 'בלי סוכר' confirms you want it pure.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Put sugar in your coffee?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: No, no sugar at all, thanks!

exampleSentence.hebrew: אֲנִי תָּמִיד שׁוֹתֶה תֵּה וְקָפֶה בְּלִי סֻכָּר!
exampleSentence.spoken: Ani tamid shote te vekafe bli sukar!
exampleSentence.english: I always drink tea and coffee without sugar!
exampleSentence.tts: אֲנִי תָּמִיד שׁוֹתֶה קָפֶה בְּלִי סֻכָּר

street_items.situationPrompt: The barista pauses with a spoon over the sugar container: 'כַּמָּה סֻכָּר?' (How much sugar?). You prefer unsweetened. What do you say?

street_items.meaning: Mild / weak cappuccino (single light espresso shot)
street_items.streetShift: Standard Israeli espresso roasts are bold and dark. If you are sensitive to caffeine or drinking coffee late in the afternoon, order 'הפוך חלש' (mild hafuch) or 'הפוך חזק' (strong hafuch with an extra shot).

dialogue.lineHebrewA: רוֹצֶה אֶת הַקָּפֶה חָזָק אוֹ חַלָּשׁ?
dialogue.lineSpokenA: Rotze et hakafe chazak o chalash?
dialogue.lineEnglishA: Do you want the coffee strong or mild?
dialogue.ttsA: רוֹצֶה אֶת הַקָּפֶה חָזָק אוֹ חַלָּשׁ?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Mild hafuch, it's evening now!

exampleSentence.hebrew: בַּלַּיְלָה אֲנִי מַזְמִין רַק הָפוּך חַלָּשׁ!
exampleSentence.spoken: Balayla ani mazmin rak hafuch chalash!
exampleSentence.english: At night I only order a mild hafuch!
exampleSentence.tts: בַּלַּיְלָה אֲנִי מַזְמִין רַק הָפוּך חַלָּשׁ

street_items.situationPrompt: It's 6:00 PM and you want a warm milky coffee without staying awake all night. What specific drink type do you ask the barista for?
street_items.situationAudio: רוֹצֶה אֶת הַקָּפֶה חָזָק אוֹ חַלָּשׁ?

street_items.meaning: Cold / Iced (e.g. קָפֶה קַר — unsweetened iced coffee)
street_items.streetShift: Note the big cultural difference: 'קָפֶה קַר' (kafe kar) is real iced espresso over cold milk with ice cubes. In contrast, 'אַיְיס קָפֶה' (ice cafe) refers to the sweet slushy machine drink from Aroma!

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Hot or iced?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Iced, it's really hot outside today!

exampleSentence.hebrew: בַּקַּיִץ כֻּלָּם שׁוֹתִים קָפֶה קַר בַּיָּם!
exampleSentence.spoken: Bakayitz kulam shotim kafe kar bayam!
exampleSentence.english: In summer everyone drinks iced coffee at the beach!

street_items.situationPrompt: It's 34°C (93°F) in July on Bograshov St. The barista asks: 'חַם אוֹ קַר?' (Hot or iced?). What 1-word answer do you give?

street_items.meaning: Can I have the check / bill please?
street_items.streetShift: In Israel, servers almost never bring the check unprompted—it's considered rude to rush diners. You must catch the server's eye and say: 'אֶפְשָׁר חֶשְׁבּוֹן?' (or make the universal check-scribble hand gesture).

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Excuse me, can we have the bill?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Sure, bringing it right over to you!

exampleSentence.hebrew: סִיַּמְנוּ לֶאֱכֹל, אֶפְשָׁר חֶשְׁבּוֹן בְּבַקָּשָׁה?
exampleSentence.spoken: Siyamnu le'echol, efshar cheshbon bevakasha?
exampleSentence.english: We finished eating, can we have the check please?

street_items.situationPrompt: You and your friends finished dinner. Plates have been cleared for 20 minutes and you want to leave. What phrase do you call to the server?

street_items.meaning: Close my tab / finalize my bill (literally: close for me)
street_items.streetShift: At lively Tel Aviv bars and pubs where you gave a card to open an open tab, say to the bartender: 'תִּסְגֹּר לִי!' (close my tab) instead of the formal 'אפשר חשבון'.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Bro, close my tab over at the bar!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Done man, eighty shekels!

exampleSentence.hebrew: אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ, תִּסְגֹּר לִי אֶת הַחֶשְׁבּוֹן!
exampleSentence.spoken: Ani holech, tisgor li et hacheshbon!
exampleSentence.english: I'm leaving, close my tab for me!
exampleSentence.tts: אֲנִי הוֹלֵךְ, תִּסְגֹּר לִי אֶת הַחֶשְׁבּוֹן

street_items.situationPrompt: You're at a crowded neighborhood pub in Florentin and ready to leave. You opened a tab with your name on it. What casual 2-word phrase do you say to the bartender?

street_items.meaning: Credit card or cash?
street_items.streetShift: Israel is virtually 95% cashless today (Apple Pay, contactless chip, and Bit app dominate). Still, servers and cashiers always ask 'אַשְׁרַאי אוֹ מְזֻמָּן?' to set up the terminal.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Credit card or cash?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Credit please, on my phone!

exampleSentence.hebrew: אֶפְשָׁר לְשַׁלֵּם בְּאַשְׁרַאי, אוֹ רַק מְזֻמָּן?
exampleSentence.spoken: Efshar leshalem be'ashrai, o rak mezuman?
exampleSentence.english: Can I pay by credit card, or only cash?

street_items.situationPrompt: You step up to pay at a boutique. The cashier holds the portable credit terminal and asks: 'אַשְׁרַאי אוֹ מְזֻמָּן?'. What is she asking?
street_items.situationCorrect: Whether you want to pay by credit card or cash
situationDistractors: Whether you want to sit inside or outside
Whether you want a paper receipt or SMS
Whether you want hot or cold coffee

street_items.meaning: Tip included inside (added to card charge)
street_items.streetShift: Standard tipping in Israeli dining is 12% to 15%. When handing your card to the server, you say 'טִיפּ בִּפְנִים!' or tell them the total amount including tip (e.g., 'תעשה שמונים עם הטיפ').

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Should I add service onto the card?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: כֵּן, תּוֹסִיף חֲמִשָּׁה-עָשָׂר אָחוּז, טִיפּ בִּפְנִים!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Ken, tosif chamisha-asar achuz, tip bif-ním!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Yes, add 15%, tip included inside!

exampleSentence.hebrew: שִׁלַּמְתִּי מֵאָה שֶׁקֶל כּוֹלֵל טִיפּ בִּפְנִים!
exampleSentence.spoken: Shilamti me'a shekel kolel tip bifnim!
exampleSentence.english: I paid 100 shekels including the tip inside!

street_items.situationPrompt: The server presents the card terminal with your 90 NIS bill. You want to round it to 105 NIS so the 15 NIS tip is charged directly to your card. What phrase do you tell him?

street_items.meaning: Bit (Israel's universal peer-to-peer phone payment app)
street_items.streetShift: Bit (by Bank Hapoalim) is so ubiquitous in Israel that it became an everyday verb: 'תַּבְיֵיט לִי' (Bit me the money!). Small corner shops, markets, barbers, and friends split bills via Bit 24/7.

dialogue.lineHebrewA: אֵין לִי מְזֻמָּן, אֵיךְ לְהַחְזִיר לְךָ?
dialogue.lineSpokenA: Ein li mezuman, eich lehachzir lecha?
dialogue.lineEnglishA: I don't have cash, how should I pay you back?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Just transfer it to me on Bit!

exampleSentence.hebrew: שָׁלַחְתִּי לְךָ חֲמִשִּׁים שֶׁקֶל בְּבִּיט עַל הַפִּיצָה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Shalachti lecha chamishim shekel be-Bit al hapitza!
exampleSentence.english: I sent you 50 shekels on Bit for the pizza!

street_items.situationPrompt: You covered your coworker's lunch bill. He opens his wallet and realizes he has no cash. What universal Israeli app do you tell him to use?

street_items.meaning: Receipt via SMS text message?
street_items.streetShift: Israeli retail laws allow stores to avoid printing paper receipts. At Super-Pharm, Shufersal, and AM:PM, the cashier will prompt 'קַבָּלָה בְּסִמְס אוֹ מֻדְפֶּסֶת?' (SMS or printed receipt?).

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Want receipt via SMS text to your phone?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: No thanks, no need!

exampleSentence.hebrew: אֲנִי תָּמִיד לוֹקֵחַ קַבָּלָה בְּסִמְס כְּדֵי לִשְׁמֹר עַל הַסְּבִיבָה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Ani tamid lokeach kabala be-SMS kedei lishmor al hasviva!
exampleSentence.english: I always take an SMS receipt to save the environment!

street_items.situationPrompt: You pay for sunscreen at Super-Pharm. The cashier types your number and asks: 'קַבָּלָה בְּסִמְס?'. What is he asking?
street_items.situationCorrect: Whether you want your sales receipt texted to your phone
situationDistractors: Whether you want to pay with credit or cash
Whether you need a shopping cart
Whether you have a club membership discount

street_items.meaning: Do you need a shopping bag? (Costs 10 agorot by law)
street_items.streetShift: Israeli law mandates a small fee for plastic shopping bags at grocery stores. The cashier will always ask 'צָרִיךְ שַׂקִּית?' (need a bag?) so they know whether to add the fee to your total.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Do you need a bag for the groceries?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: No thanks, I brought a backpack from home!

exampleSentence.hebrew: שַׂקִּית אַחַת בְּבַקָּשָׁה, יֵשׁ לִי הַרְבֵּה דְּבָרִים!
exampleSentence.spoken: Sakit achat bevakasha, yesh li harbe dvarim!
exampleSentence.english: One bag please, I have many items!

street_items.situationPrompt: At the checkout register, the clerk has bagged nothing and asks: 'צָרִיךְ שַׂקִּית?'. What is she asking you?
street_items.situationCorrect: Do you need a shopping bag? (fee applies)
situationDistractors: Do you need directions to the bus stop?

street_items.meaning: Gett (Israel's universal taxi-hailing app)
street_items.streetShift: Uber in Israel works almost entirely with licensed taxis through Gett. Saying 'בוא נזמין גט' (let's order a Gett) is the universal way to summon a cab from your phone.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: How will we get to the beach now?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: נַזְמִין גֶּט, מַגִּיעַ עוֹד שְׁתֵּי דַּקּוֹת!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Nazmin Gett, magia od shtei dakot!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Let's order a Gett, arriving in 2 minutes!

exampleSentence.hebrew: הִזְמַנְתִּי גֶּט, הַנַּהָג כְּבָר לְמַטָּה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Hizmanti Gett, hanahag kvar lemata!
exampleSentence.english: I ordered a Gett, the driver is already downstairs!

street_items.situationPrompt: You and your friends are leaving a party late at night with no buses running. How do you propose hailing a ride via smartphone?

street_items.meaning: Taximeter (insisting on the legal meter fare)
street_items.streetShift: Israeli taxi drivers legally must run the meter, but often try to quote fixed inflated flat rates ('שישים שקל ונסע'). Always insist firmly: 'שִׂים מוֹנֶה, בְּבַקָּשָׁה!' (Put on the meter, please).
street_items.scene: 🚕 Taxi Window, Tel Aviv Central Station

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Fifty shekels and we go straight away?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: No thanks, put on the meter please!

exampleSentence.hebrew: תָּמִיד כְּדַאי לִנְסֹעַ עִם מוֹנֶה בְּתֵל אָבִיב!
exampleSentence.spoken: Tamid kedai linsoa im mone betel aviv!
exampleSentence.english: It's always better to ride with a meter in Tel Aviv!

street_items.situationPrompt: You get into a taxi outside the train station. The driver offers a fixed 70 NIS flat price. What assertive phrase ensures you pay the fair legal fare?

street_items.meaning: Are you free / available? (Asked to taxi driver)
street_items.streetShift: When flagging a taxi curbside, lean down to the front passenger window and ask 'אַתָּה פָּנוּי?' before opening the rear door and getting inside.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Hello, are you free for a trip to Jaffa?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Yes man, get in!

exampleSentence.hebrew: סְלִיחָה נַהָג, אַתָּה פָּנוּי עַכְשָׁו?
exampleSentence.spoken: Slicha nahag, ata panui achshav?
exampleSentence.english: Excuse me driver, are you available now?

street_items.situationPrompt: A white taxi rolls up slowly to the curb with its rooftop light on. You peek in the front window. What polite question do you ask the driver?

street_items.meaning: How much is it to...?
street_items.streetShift: Before committing to a long intercity or airport trip, ask 'כַּמָּה זֶה עַד?' plus your destination (e.g. 'כמה זה עד ירושלים?').

dialogue.lineEnglishA: How much is it to the airport?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: 150 shekels on the meter!

exampleSentence.hebrew: כַּמָּה זֶה עַד הַתַּחֲנָה הַמֶּרְכָּזִית?
exampleSentence.spoken: Kama ze ad hatachana hamerkazit?
exampleSentence.english: How much is it to the central bus station?

street_items.situationPrompt: You need to know the approximate cab fare before hopping in for a ride to Jerusalem. What formula do you use?

street_items.meaning: Straight ahead / Keep going straight
street_items.streetShift: Doubling words for emphasis is very typical of Israeli speech rhythm. 'ישר ישר' means 'don't turn anywhere yet, just keep driving straight down this avenue'.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Where now, turn here?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Keep going straight straight all the way to the sea!

exampleSentence.hebrew: תֵּלֵךְ יָשָׁר יָשָׁר וְתִרְאֶה אֶת הַבַּנְק מִצַּד יָמִין!
exampleSentence.spoken: Telech yashar yashar vetir'e et habank mitzad yamin!
exampleSentence.english: Walk straight ahead and you'll see the bank on the right!

street_items.situationPrompt: The driver slows down approaching an intersection and asks which way to turn. You want him to continue straight without turning. What do you instruct?

street_items.meaning: Right at the traffic light
street_items.streetShift: Giving advance notice to Israeli cab drivers is key before they enter the wrong lane. Say 'יְמִינָה בָּרַמְזוֹר' well before the intersection so they can merge right.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Where should I turn bro?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Take a right at the next traffic light!

exampleSentence.hebrew: בָּרַמְזוֹר תִּפְנֶה יְמִינָה לִרְחוֹב אַלֶנְבִּי!
exampleSentence.spoken: Baramzor tifne yemina lirchov allenby!
exampleSentence.english: At the traffic light turn right onto Allenby street!

street_items.situationPrompt: The cab driver is in the center lane and asks where your turn is. You need him to turn right at the upcoming signals. What do you call out?

street_items.meaning: To the left / Turn left
street_items.streetShift: 'שְׂמֹאלָה' (smóla) means toward the left. Note the direction suffix '-ah' which converts nouns of direction into movements (יָמִין -> יְמִינָה, שְׂמֹאל -> שְׂמֹאלָה).

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Turn right at the roundabout?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: No, left at the roundabout please!

exampleSentence.hebrew: בַּסּוֹף שֶׁל הָרְחוֹב תִּקַּח שְׂמֹאלָה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Basof shel harechov tikach smola!
exampleSentence.english: At the end of the street take a left!

street_items.situationPrompt: The driver asks if he should turn right at the square. You need him to turn left. What 1-word direction command do you say?

street_items.meaning: Right here at the corner (drop me off)
street_items.streetShift: Instead of having a taxi crawl down a one-way congested side street, Israelis usually say 'תּוֹרִיד אוֹתִי פֹּה בַּפִּנָּה!' (drop me right here at the corner) to save time and money.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Where exactly is your address?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: תּוֹרִיד אוֹתִי פֹּה בַּפִּנָּה, זֶה מְצֻיָּן!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Torid oti po ba-pi-ná, ze metzuyan!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Drop me right here at the corner, that's perfect!

exampleSentence.hebrew: אַתָּה יָכוֹל לַעֲצֹר לִי פֹּה בַּפִּנָּה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Ata yachol la'atzor li po bapina!
exampleSentence.english: You can stop for me right here at the corner!

street_items.situationPrompt: You see your destination 20 meters ahead, but traffic is backing up before the alley. How do you tell the driver to let you out right at the intersection?

street_items.meaning: Rav-Kav (Israel's national transit smartcard)
street_items.streetShift: Israeli buses and trains no longer accept cash onboard. You must tap a 'רַב-קַו' (Rav-Kav) smartcard or scan a transit app (Moovit / HopOn) upon boarding.
street_items.scene: 🚌 Boarding Dan Bus Line 5, Tel Aviv

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Did you validate with Rav-Kav or app?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: כֵּן, הִנֵּה הָרַב-קַו שֶׁלִּי, תִּקַּפְתִּי כְּבָר!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Ken, hine harav-kav sheli, tikafti kvar!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Yes, here's my Rav-Kav, I already validated!

exampleSentence.hebrew: צָרִיךְ לְהַטְעִין אֶת הָרַב-קַו לִפְנֵי שֶׁעוֹלִים לָאוֹטוֹבּוּס!
exampleSentence.spoken: Tsarich lehat'in et harav-kav lifnei she'olim la'otobus!
exampleSentence.english: You need to reload your Rav-Kav before boarding the bus!

street_items.situationPrompt: A transit ticket inspector boards the bus and asks all passengers to present their payment card. What item do you show him?

street_items.meaning: Next station / next stop
street_items.streetShift: This phrase is broadcast over the loudspeaker before every bus and train stop across the country: 'הַתַּחֲנָה הַבָּאָה: רַכֶּבֶת הַשָּׁלוֹם'.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: The next station: Yehudit Boulevard!
dialogue.lineHebrewB: אָחִי, אֲנִי יוֹרֵד בַּתַּחֲנָה הַבָּאָה, תֵּן לַעֲבֹר!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Achi, ani yored batachana haba'a, ten la'avor!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Bro, I'm getting off at the next stop, let me pass!

exampleSentence.hebrew: נַהָג, אַתָּה עוֹצֵר בַּתַּחֲנָה הַבָּאָה?
exampleSentence.spoken: Nahag, ata otzer batachana haba'a?
exampleSentence.english: Driver, are you stopping at the next stop?

street_items.situationPrompt: You hear the bus automated voice chime: 'הַתַּחֲנָה הַבָּאָה...'. What is it alerting passengers to?
situationDistractors: The bus driver's shift has ended
The ticket price is going up

street_items.meaning: Sherut (Shared yellow minivan taxi, e.g. Monit Sherut)
street_items.streetShift: 'מוֹנִית שֵׁרוּת' are 10-seater yellow minivans following bus routes. Crucially, sherut vans run on Shabbat (Friday night & Saturday) when regular public buses shut down!

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Yes, there is an open seat in back, hop on!
dialogue.lineHebrewB: כֵּן, יֵשׁ מָקוֹם פָּנוּי מֵאָחוֹר, תַּעֲלֶה!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Ken, yesh makom panui me'achor, ta'ale!

exampleSentence.hebrew: בְּשַׁבָּת אֵין אוֹטוֹבּוּסִים אָז אֲנִי נוֹסֵעַ בְּשֵׁרוּת!
exampleSentence.spoken: Beshabat ein otobusim az ani nose'a besherut!
exampleSentence.english: On Shabbat there are no buses, so I ride a sherut minivan!

street_items.situationPrompt: It's Saturday afternoon and buses are not running. You need to get from Tel Aviv to Netanya or along Ben Yehuda St. What shared transit van do you look for?

street_items.meaning: 'I feel like / I'm craving' (literally: it comes to me)
street_items.streetShift: Israelis rarely use the formal verb 'אֲנִי רוֹצֶה' (I want) when talking about food, cravings, or spontaneous ideas. Instead, they say 'בָּא לִי!' (I feel like / craving).

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Bro, what are we eating today for lunch?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: מַמָּשׁ בָּא לִי שַׁוַארְמָה עִם הַרְבֵּה טְחִינָה!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Mamash ba li shavarma im harbe tchina!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: I'm really craving shawarma with plenty of tahini!

exampleSentence.hebrew: בָּא לִי לָלֶכֶת לַיָּם עַכְשָׁו!
exampleSentence.spoken: Ba li lalechet layam achshav!
exampleSentence.english: I feel like going to the beach right now!

street_items.situationPrompt: Your friend asks what you feel like eating. You have a sudden urge for hot falafel. How do you express this craving like a true local?

street_items.meaning: 'I don't feel like it / I'm not in the mood'
street_items.streetShift: The quintessential Israeli phrase for declining invitations or activities when you just aren't in the mood: 'לֹא בָּא לִי!' (I don't feel like it). Direct, honest, and universally understood.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Do you feel like going out to the party tonight?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: מַמָּשׁ לֹא בָּא לִי, אֲנִי גָּמוּר מֵעֲיֵפוּת!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Mamash lo ba li, ani gamur me'ayefut!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: I really don't feel like it, I'm wiped out!

exampleSentence.hebrew: לֹא בָּא לִי לְבַשֵּׁל הַיּוֹם, נַזְמִין מַשֶּׁהוּ!
exampleSentence.spoken: Lo ba li levashel hayom, nazmin mashehu!
exampleSentence.english: I don't feel like cooking today, let's order in!

street_items.situationPrompt: Someone invites you to a crowded bar on a rainy Tuesday, but you just want to stay in bed and watch TV. How do you decline naturally?

street_items.meaning: 'No way! / Absolutely no chance' (literally: there is no situation)
street_items.streetShift: 'אֵין מַצָּב' is Israel's #1 emphatic refusal. It translates to 'under no circumstances / impossible / no way in hell!'.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Will you come to the office on Friday morning?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: אֵין מַצָּב בָּעוֹלָם, זֶה יוֹם הַחֹפֶשׁ שֶׁלִּי!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Ein matzav ba'olam, ze yom hachofesh sheli!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: No way in the world, that's my day off!

exampleSentence.hebrew: אֵין מַצָּב שֶׁנַּסְפִּיק אֶת הָרַכֶּבֶת, הִיא כְּבָר יוֹצֵאת!
exampleSentence.spoken: Ein matzav shenaspik et harakevet, hi kvar yotzet!
exampleSentence.english: No way we catch the train, it's already leaving!

street_items.situationPrompt: Someone asks if you're willing to pay 100 shekels for a single cup of lukewarm tea. What emphatic refusal do you blurt out?

street_items.meaning: 'There's a chance / Quite possible / Definite maybe'
street_items.streetShift: The flip side of 'אין מצב'. 'יֵשׁ מַצָּב' means 'there's a real possibility / probably yes / it could happen'.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Are we seeing you at the bar tonight?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: יֵשׁ מַצָּב, תְּעַדְכֵּן אוֹתִי כְּשֶׁאַתֶּם שָׁם!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Yesh matz-záv, te'adken oti kshe'atem sham!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: There's a good chance, text me when you get there!

exampleSentence.hebrew: יֵשׁ מַצָּב שֶׁיֵּרֵד גֶּשֶׁם מָחָר בַּבֹּקֶר!
exampleSentence.spoken: Yesh matzav sheyered geshem machar baboker!
exampleSentence.english: There's a good chance it'll rain tomorrow morning!

street_items.situationPrompt: A friend asks if you'll join them at the concert on Friday. You're 80% likely to go if you finish work early. What phrase conveys this?

street_items.meaning: 'Say... / Tell me...' (Conversational opening to a male)
street_items.streetShift: When addressing any man on the street to ask a question, Israelis begin with 'תַּגִּיד...' (Say...). It instantly softens the question and grabs attention.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Say bro, what time is it?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: 3:30, champ!

exampleSentence.hebrew: תַּגִּיד, אַתָּה יוֹדֵעַ אֵיפֹה יֵשׁ כַּסְפּוֹמָט פֹּה?
exampleSentence.spoken: Tagid, ata yode'a eifo yesh kaspomat po?
exampleSentence.english: Say, do you know where there's an ATM here?

street_items.situationPrompt: You need to ask a male passerby on the street for directions. What word do you open your sentence with?

street_items.meaning: 'Say... / Tell me...' (Conversational opening to a female)
street_items.streetShift: The feminine equivalent of 'תַּגִּיד'. When asking a woman for the time, directions, or her opinion, open with 'תַּגִּידִי...'.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Say, does this bus line reach the train station?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Yes, get off at the 3rd stop!

exampleSentence.hebrew: תַּגִּידִי, מָה דַּעְתֵּךְ עַל הַמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה?
exampleSentence.spoken: Tagidi, ma da'tech al hamakom haze?
exampleSentence.english: Say, what's your take on this place?

street_items.situationPrompt: You want to ask a woman waiting at the bus stop if the #5 bus already passed. What word begins your sentence?

street_items.meaning: 'What on earth?! / Are you kidding?! / No way!'
street_items.streetShift: Literally 'what suddenly?'. In reality, 'מָה פִּתְאוֹם!' is the ultimate Israeli exclamation of indignance, shock, or disbelief: 'Are you crazy?! No way!'

dialogue.lineEnglishA: I heard you're leaving the country?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: מָה פִּתְאוֹם?! מִי סִפֵּר לְךָ אֶת זֶה?! אֲנִי נִשְׁאָר פֹּה!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Ma pit-óm?! Mi siper lecha et ze?! Ani nish'ar po!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: What on earth?! Who told you that?! I'm staying right here!

exampleSentence.hebrew: מָה פִּתְאוֹם שֶׁנְּשַׁלֵּם מָחָר, נְשַׁלֵּם עַכְשָׁו!
exampleSentence.spoken: Ma pit'om sheneshalem machar, neshalem achshav!
exampleSentence.english: No way we pay tomorrow, let's pay right now!

street_items.situationPrompt: A coworker spreads a rumor that you are resigning next week. You are stunned and completely deny it. What classic exclamation do you make?

street_items.meaning: 'Terrible / Awful / In shambles' (literally: on the face)
street_items.streetShift: When something is a disaster—food was tasteless, service was horrific, weather is miserable, or you feel sick—Israelis say it is 'עַל הַפָּנִים!' (faceplanted / terrible).

dialogue.lineEnglishA: How was the movie you saw?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: הָיָה עַל הַפָּנִים, מַמָּשׁ בִּזְבּוּז שֶׁל זְמַן!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Haya al ha-pa-ním, mamash bizbuz shel zman!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: It was terrible, a total waste of time!

exampleSentence.hebrew: הַשֵּׁרוּת שָׁם הָיָה עַל הַפָּנִים, לֹא חוֹזֵר לְשָׁם!
exampleSentence.spoken: Hasherut sham haya al hapanim, lo chozer lesham!
exampleSentence.english: The service there was awful, I'm never going back!

street_items.situationPrompt: You tried a newly opened restaurant that served cold soggy food and overcharged you. A friend asks how it was. What candid slang review do you give?

street_items.meaning: 'Let's go! / Come on! / Wrap it up'
street_items.streetShift: Originally Arabic, 'יַאלְלָה' is Israel's universally spoken motor word: 'יאללה נזוז' (let's get moving), 'יאללה ביי' (alright bye), or 'יאללה תביא' (come on, hand it over).

dialogue.lineEnglishA: So when are we hitting the road?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Let's go, get up, it's already late!

exampleSentence.hebrew: יַאלְלָה, בּוֹאוּ נִסְגֹּר חֶשְׁבּוֹן וְנֵלֵךְ!
exampleSentence.spoken: Yalla, bo'u nisgor cheshbon venelech!
exampleSentence.english: Come on, let's close the check and go!

street_items.situationPrompt: You are sitting with friends who are dawdling while the movie starts in 10 minutes. What high-energy word do you use to rally everyone up?

street_items.meaning: 'Bottom line / Let's get to the point / Realistically'
street_items.streetShift: Originally Yiddish (from Hebrew 'תַּכְלִית' - purpose). 'תכל'ס' is the cornerstone of Israeli pragmatism. It cuts through chit-chat: 'Cut the nonsense, what's the bottom line?'.
street_items.scene: 💼 Startup Meeting / Cafe Chat, Tel Aviv

dialogue.lineEnglishA: So what was the conclusion with him in the end?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Bottom line, he was 100% right!

exampleSentence.hebrew: בּוֹא נְדַבֵּר תַּכְלֶ'ס, כַּמָּה זֶה עוֹלֶה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Bo nedaber tachles, kama ze ole?
exampleSentence.english: Let's talk bottom line, how much does it actually cost?
exampleSentence.tts: בּוֹא נְדַבֵּר תַּכְלֶס, כַּמָּה זֶה עוֹלֶה?

street_items.situationPrompt: A vendor is giving a long windy sales speech about a phone plan. You want the raw facts without the fluff. What quintessential Israeli word do you invoke?

street_items.meaning: 'Awesome / Great / Cool / Sounds good'
street_items.streetShift: Originally Arabic (meaning great/fine). 'סַבָּבָה' is Israel's most ubiquitous slang word. It functions as 'cool', 'sounds like a plan', 'no problem', or 'I'm good'.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Meet at 7 at the beach for sunset?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Totally cool, see you there!

exampleSentence.hebrew: הַכֹּל סַבָּבָה, אֵין מָה לִדְאֹג!
exampleSentence.spoken: Hakol sababa, ein ma lid'og!
exampleSentence.english: Everything is great, nothing to worry about!

street_items.situationPrompt: A friend proposes getting pizza and drinks on Thursday evening. You are totally on board with the plan. What 1-word slang agreement do you reply?

street_items.meaning: 'Cool / Slick / Impressive'
street_items.streetShift: Derived from the root ג-נ-ב (to steal/sneak), 'מַגְנִיב' means something that steals your attention—clever, stylish, or impressive.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: I bought a cool new electric guitar yesterday!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Wow, super cool, show me!

exampleSentence.hebrew: זֶה רַעְיוֹן מַמָּשׁ מַגְנִיב, בּוֹא נַעֲשֶׂה אֶת זֶה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Ze ra'ayon mamash magniv, bo na'ase et ze!
exampleSentence.english: That's a really cool idea, let's do it!

street_items.situationPrompt: Someone demonstrates a slick smartphone shortcut that solves your problem in 2 seconds. What word praises the feature as cool and clever?

street_items.meaning: 'Awesome / Great / Superb' (e.g. אחלה מקום)
street_items.streetShift: From Arabic 'aḥlā' (sweetest/best). Israelis use 'אַחְלָה' as an adjective placed before nouns: 'אחלה בן אדם' (a great guy), 'אחלה רעיון' (great idea), or standalone 'אחלה!' (great!).

dialogue.lineEnglishA: How is that restaurant you heard about?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: אַחְלָה מָקוֹם, שֵׁרוּת פְּצָצָה וְאוֹכֶל מְעֻלֶּה!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Ách-la makom, sherut petzatza ve'ochel me'ule!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Superb place, bomb service and excellent food!

exampleSentence.hebrew: דָּנִי הוּא אַחְלָה גֶּבֶר, תָּמִיד עוֹזֵר לְכֻלָּם!
exampleSentence.spoken: Dani hu achla gever, tamid ozer lekulam!
exampleSentence.english: Dani is a great guy, always helps everyone!

street_items.situationPrompt: You want to recommend a rooftop hangout to your friend as a great spot with good music. What phrase do you use?

street_items.meaning: 'Fire! / Awesome! / Super exciting!'
street_items.streetShift: Just like 'fire / lit' in modern English slang, young Israelis shout 'אֵשׁ!' when plans are confirmed, when a DJ drops a banger track, or when great news arrives.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: I scored us tickets to the big match on Saturday!
dialogue.lineHebrewB: אֵשׁ! אַתָּה תּוֹתָח, כַּמָּה אֲנִי חַיָּב לְךָ!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Esh! Ata totach, kama ani chayav lecha?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Fire! You're a legend, how much do I owe you?

exampleSentence.hebrew: הָיְתָה מְסִבָּה אֵשׁ אֶתְמוֹל בַּלַּיְלָה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Hayta mesiba esh etmol balayla!
exampleSentence.english: It was a lit / fire party last night!

street_items.situationPrompt: Your friend texts that your group just got VIP access to an exclusive DJ set. What 1-word reaction expresses maximum hype?

street_items.meaning: 'A total mess / Chaos / Wild disorder'
street_items.streetShift: Originally from Russian/Persian (puppet booth / uproar), 'בָּלָגָן' is Israel's defining sociological term. Traffic jams, disorganized events, unruly crowds, or a messy room are all 'בָּלָגָן'.
street_items.scene: 🌪️ Central Bus Station Traffic, Tel Aviv

dialogue.lineEnglishA: What's going on over there on the road?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: בָּלָגָן שָׁלֵם, שְׁנֵי אוֹטוֹבּוּסִים חָסְמוּ אֶת הַכֹּל!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Ba-la-gán shalem, shnei otobusim chasmu et hakol!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Total chaos, two buses blocked everything!

exampleSentence.hebrew: יֵשׁ לִי בָּלָגָן בַּחֶדֶר, אֲנִי חַיָּב לְסַדֵּר!
exampleSentence.spoken: Yesh li balagan bacheder, ani chayav lesader!
exampleSentence.english: I have a total mess in my room, I have to tidy up!

street_items.situationPrompt: You walk into an airport terminal where flights are delayed, bags are piled high, and everyone is shouting over each other. How do you summarize the scene?

street_items.meaning: 'Just kidding / For no reason / Not serious / Just because'
street_items.streetShift: 'סְתָם' is a magical Israeli word. After a prank: 'סְתָם!' (just kidding!). When asked why you called: 'סְתָם, רָצִיתִי לִשְׁמֹעַ מָה נִשְׁמַע' (no reason, just wanted to say hi).

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Why did you ask that question?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Just because, not really anything important!

exampleSentence.hebrew: אַל תִּתְרַגֵּשׁ מִמֶּנּוּ, הוּא סְתָם צוֹחֵק!
exampleSentence.spoken: Al titragesh mimenu, hu stam tzochek!
exampleSentence.english: Don't get upset with him, he's just joking around!

street_items.situationPrompt: You tease a colleague with a mock-serious face, then smile so they know you weren't serious. What word immediately reveals you were just joking?

street_items.meaning: 'Actually / Specifically / Contrary to expectations'
street_items.streetShift: Originally Aramaic ('precisely'). In Israeli Hebrew, 'דַּוְקָא' is used when reality defies expectations: 'Everyone said the movie sucked, but דַּוְקָא I loved it!'.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: The exam was probably very difficult?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Actually, contrary to expectations, it was really fair and easy!

exampleSentence.hebrew: דַּוְקָא הַיּוֹם לֹא יוֹרֵד גֶּשֶׁם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ!
exampleSentence.spoken: Davka hayom lo yored geshem kmo she'amru!
exampleSentence.english: Actually today it's not raining like they said it would!

street_items.situationPrompt: Everyone warned you that the new restaurant had bad reviews, but your meal turned out to be delicious. What nuance word introduces your pleasant surprise?

street_items.meaning: 'Really? / Wow / I see / No kidding!'
street_items.streetShift: From Arabic 'wa-llāh' (by God). 'וַאלְלָה' changes meaning with intonation: rising 'וַאלְלָה?' = 'Really?! No kidding!'; falling 'וַאלְלָה...' = 'I see / Gotcha'.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: I started studying Hebrew every single day!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Really?! Respect bro, best of luck!

exampleSentence.hebrew: וַאלְלָה, לֹא יָדַעְתִּי שֶׁאַתָּה גָּר פֹּה בַּשְּׁכוּנָה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Walla, lo yadati she'ata gar po bashchuna!
exampleSentence.english: Really, I had no idea you live here in the neighborhood!
exampleSentence.tts: וַאלְלָה, לֹא יָדַעְתִּי שֶׁאַתָּה גָּר פֹּה

street_items.situationPrompt: An acquaintance tells you they just bought an apartment right down your street. What 1-word reaction expresses genuine surprise and interest?

street_items.meaning: 'Darling / Honey / Sweetheart' (e.g. כפרה עליך)
street_items.streetShift: Originally referring to the Yom Kippur atonement ritual, 'כַּפָּרָה עָלֶיךָ' (kapara alecha) evolved into Israel's warmest, most affectionate slang term: 'my sweetheart / bless your soul!'.
street_items.scene: 👵 Grandmother's Kitchen / Market Stall, Shuk HaTikva

dialogue.lineHebrewA: תּוֹדָה רַבָּה שֶׁעֲזַרְתָּ לִי עִם הַסַּלִּים!
dialogue.lineSpokenA: Toda raba she'azarta li im hasalim!
dialogue.lineEnglishA: Thank you so much for helping me carry the market baskets!
dialogue.lineHebrewB: בְּכֵיף, כַּפָּרָה עָלַיִךְ, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה יוֹם מַקְסִים!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Bekef, ka-pa-ra alayich, sheyihye yom maksim!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: With pleasure darling, have a wonderful day!

exampleSentence.hebrew: בּוֹא שֵׁב תֹּאכַל מַשֶּׁהוּ, כַּפָּרָה עָלֶיךָ!
exampleSentence.spoken: Bo shev tochal mashehu, kapara alecha!
exampleSentence.english: Come sit eat something, sweetheart / bless you!

street_items.situationPrompt: An elderly lady in the market smiles warmly after you help her reach the top shelf and calls you 'כפרה עליך'. What emotion is she expressing?
street_items.situationCorrect: Deep affection, gratitude, and blessing ('Darling / Bless your soul')
situationDistractors: She is scolding you for dropping a fruit
She is asking you for change for a 50 shekel bill
She is telling you the store is closed

street_items.meaning: 'Living in a movie / Delusional / Out of touch with reality'
street_items.streetShift: When someone makes absurdly unrealistic demands, has an overinflated ego, or expects miracles, Israelis say: 'אַתָּה חַי בְּסֶרֶט!' (You're living in a fantasy movie!).

dialogue.lineHebrewA: הוּא דּוֹרֵשׁ עֲשֶׂרֶת אֲלָפִים שֶׁקֶל עַל דִּירַת חֶדֶר מִתְפָּרֶקֶת!
dialogue.lineSpokenA: Hu doresh aseret alafim shekel al dirat cheder mitpareket!
dialogue.lineEnglishA: He's demanding 10,000 NIS for a crumbling studio apartment!
dialogue.lineHebrewB: הוּא מַמָּשׁ חַי בְּסֶרֶט, אַף אֶחָד לֹא יִשְׂכֹּר אֶת זֶה!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Hu mamash chai be-sé-ret, af echad lo yiskor et ze!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: He is truly living in a fantasy movie, nobody will rent that!

exampleSentence.hebrew: אִם אַתָּה חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁתִּמְצָא חֲנָיָה בְּתֵל אָבִיב בְּשַׁבָּת, אַתָּה חַי בְּסֶרֶט!
exampleSentence.spoken: Im ata choshev shetimtza chanaya betel aviv beshabat, ata chai beseret!
exampleSentence.english: If you think you'll find parking in Tel Aviv on Saturday, you're delusional!
exampleSentence.tts: אַתָּה חַי בְּסֶרֶט אִם תַּחְשֹׁב כָּכָה

street_items.situationPrompt: A friend claims he will become a millionaire next month without working. What classic Israeli phrase tells him he's completely detached from reality?

street_items.meaning: 'Bro / My brother' (Universal informal address)
street_items.streetShift: 'אָחִי' is used dozens of times a day in Israel to greet strangers, cashiers, friends, drivers, and waiters. It establishes instant warm egalitarian rapport.

dialogue.lineHebrewA: אָחִי, מָה נִשְׁמַע, יֵשׁ מַיִם קָרִים?
dialogue.lineSpokenA: A-chí, ma nishma, yesh mayim karim?
dialogue.lineEnglishA: Bro, how's it going, do you have cold water?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Sure bro, in the fridge in the back!

exampleSentence.hebrew: תּוֹדָה רַבָּה אָחִי, עָזַרְתָּ לִי מְאוֹד!
exampleSentence.spoken: Toda raba achi, azarta li me'od!
exampleSentence.english: Thanks a lot bro, you helped me so much!

street_items.situationPrompt: You walk up to a street kiosk to buy water. What universal friendly address word instantly builds warm rapport with the guy behind the counter?

street_items.meaning: 'Man / Buddy / Champ' (Addressing a male)
street_items.streetShift: Literally 'man'. Used as friendly address to any guy ('תודה גבר' — thanks man). When someone does you a huge favor, calling them 'גבר-גבר' means 'a true mensch / absolute legend'.

dialogue.lineHebrewA: תּוֹדָה רַבָּה שֶׁשָּׁמַרְתָּ לִי אֶת הַחֲנָיָה, גֶּבֶר!
dialogue.lineSpokenA: Toda raba sheshamarta li et hachanaya, gé-ver!
dialogue.lineEnglishA: Thanks so much for saving the parking spot for me, man!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: With pleasure man, have a great day!

exampleSentence.hebrew: אַתָּה גֶּבֶר אֲמִתִּי, אֵין עָלֶיךָ!
exampleSentence.spoken: Ata gever amiti, ein alecha!
exampleSentence.english: You're a true mensch / real champ, you're unbeatable!

street_items.situationPrompt: A guy holds the elevator door open when your hands are full of bags. How do you thank him casually as a peer?

street_items.meaning: 'Sweetie / Honey / Dear'
street_items.streetShift: Derived from 'מָתוֹק' (sweet). Friendly servers, market sellers, and friends frequently address people as 'מוֹתֶק' (sweetie).

dialogue.lineEnglishA: What would you like to eat this morning, sweetie?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: רַק קְרוּאָסוֹן חַם וְקָפֶה קָטָן, תּוֹדָה!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Rak croissant cham vekafe katan, toda!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Just a warm croissant and small coffee, thanks!

exampleSentence.hebrew: בֹּקֶר טוֹב מוֹתֶק, אֵיךְ יָשַׁנְתָּ הַלַּיְלָה!
exampleSentence.spoken: Boker tov motek, eich yashanta halayla?
exampleSentence.english: Good morning sweetie, how did you sleep last night?

street_items.situationPrompt: The friendly barista at your local morning cafe greets you with a warm smile: 'מָה בִּשְׁבִילְךָ מוֹתֶק?'. What does 'מוֹתֶק' mean?

street_items.meaning: 'My friend / Pal' (Warm Arabic loanword)
street_items.streetShift: Originally Arabic 'ḥabībī' (my beloved / friend). In Israeli street culture, fruit stall owners, market vendors, and cab drivers use 'חַבִּיבִּי' to beckon customers with warmth.

dialogue.lineHebrewA: בּוֹא חַבִּיבִּי, קַח אֲבַטִּיחַ עַל הַסַּכִּין, מָתוֹק דְּבַשׁ!
dialogue.lineSpokenA: Bo cha-bí-bi, kach avati'ach al hasakin, matok dvash!
dialogue.lineEnglishA: Come my friend, taste fresh watermelon cut on the knife, sweet as honey!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Give me half a watermelon, my friend!

exampleSentence.hebrew: שְׁמַע לִי חַבִּיבִּי, הַמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה הֲכִי טוֹב בָּעִיר!
exampleSentence.spoken: Shma li chabibi, hamakom haze hachi tov ba'ir!
exampleSentence.english: Listen to me my friend, this place is the best in town!

street_items.situationPrompt: A lively fruit vendor in the Carmel Market shouts over the crowd: 'בּוֹא חַבִּיבִּי, טְעַם תּוּרְמוּס!'. What word is he using to address you warmly?

street_items.meaning: 'What's up?' (Fast youth shorthand for מָה נִשְׁמַע)
street_items.streetShift: Israelis speak fast. Instead of the full 'מָה נִשְׁמַע' (ma nishma), teenagers and young adults clip it down to 'מָה נִשְׁ?' (ma nish?). The classic answer is 'הַכֹּל טוֹב!' (all good) or 'הַכֹּל דְּבַשׁ!' (all honey!).

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Bro, what's up?
dialogue.lineEnglishB: All good, what's going on with you?

exampleSentence.hebrew: מָה נִשְׁ חֲבֵרִים, כַּמָּה זְמַן לֹא הִתְרָאֵינוּ!
exampleSentence.spoken: Ma nish chaverim, kama zman lo hitra'enu!
exampleSentence.english: What's up friends, how long since we last saw each other!

street_items.situationPrompt: You run into a close friend on the beach boardwalk. What 2-word fast spoken greeting do they shoot at you?

street_items.meaning: 'What's happening? / What's going on?'
street_items.streetShift: Along with 'מה נשמע', 'מָה קוֹרֶה?' (literally 'what is happening?') is the most natural greeting in daily Israeli life. Answer: 'הַכֹּל בְּסֵדֶר!' (everything's in order) or 'הַכֹּל רָגִיל!' (everything normal).

dialogue.lineEnglishA: Hey bro, what's happening?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: בַּדֶּרֶךְ אֵלֶיךָ, עוֹד חָמֵשׁ דַּקּוֹת אֲנִי שָׁם!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Baderech elecha, od chamesh dakot ani sham!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: On my way to you, there in 5 minutes!

exampleSentence.hebrew: מָה קוֹרֶה אָחִי, אֵיפֹה אַתֶּם יוֹשְׁבִים עַכְשָׁו?
exampleSentence.spoken: Ma kore achi, eifo atem yoshvim achshav?
exampleSentence.english: What's up bro, where are you guys sitting right now?

street_items.situationPrompt: You answer a phone call from a buddy. He says: 'שָׁלוֹם, מָה קוֹרֶה?'. What is he asking?
street_items.situationCorrect: What's happening? / How are things going?
situationDistractors: Where are you traveling next week?
Can you lend me some money?
What did you buy at the grocery store?

street_items.meaning: 'Got it / Understood / I hear you'
street_items.streetShift: When someone explains directions, explains a rule, or clarifies a plan, say 'הֵבַנְתִּי!' (got it). It signals that their explanation was crystal clear and no repetition is needed.

dialogue.lineHebrewA: תֵּלֵךְ יָשָׁר וְאָז תִּפְנֶה שְׂמֹאלָה בַּכִּכָּר!
dialogue.lineSpokenA: Telech yashar ve'az tifne smola bakikar!
dialogue.lineEnglishA: Walk straight and then turn left at the traffic circle!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Got it, thank you so much!

exampleSentence.hebrew: הֵבַנְתִּי אֶת הַבְּעָיָה, אֲנִי אֲטַפֵּל בָּהּ מִיָּד!
exampleSentence.spoken: Hevanti et habe'aya, ani atapel bah miyad!
exampleSentence.english: I understood the problem, I will take care of it right away!

street_items.situationPrompt: A coworker explains a 3-step software process to you. You understand everything perfectly. What 1-word confirmation do you give?

street_items.meaning: 'Outstanding / Top-notch / Unbeatable' (literally: end of the road)
street_items.streetShift: Literally 'the end of the road'—meaning you can search the entire world and won't find anything better. It is Israel's highest praise for exquisite food or experiences.

dialogue.lineEnglishA: How is the masabacha here, was it good?
dialogue.lineHebrewB: וָואוּ, סוֹף הַדֶּרֶךְ, הַחוּמוּס הֲכִי טָעִים שֶׁאָכַלְתִּי!
dialogue.lineSpokenB: Wow, sof ha-dé-rech, hachumus hachi taim she'achalti!
dialogue.lineEnglishB: Wow, outstanding, the tastiest hummus I've ever eaten!

exampleSentence.hebrew: הָיְתָה חֻפְשָׁה סוֹף הַדֶּרֶךְ בְּאֵילַת!
exampleSentence.spoken: Hayta chufsha sof haderech be'eilat!
exampleSentence.english: It was an unbeatable / top-notch vacation in Eilat!

street_items.situationPrompt: You just ate the most delicious fresh warm pita with tahini of your entire life. How do you describe the meal to your friends?

street_items.meaning: 'Unbelievable! / There is nothing like this in the world!'
street_items.streetShift: Literally 'no such things exist'. Israelis say this when a concert, dessert, sunset, or view is so mind-blowing that it defies imagination: 'אֵין דְּבָרִים כָּאֵלֶּה!'.

street_items.meaning: 'Alright, bye! / Take care! / Catch you later!'
street_items.streetShift: The universal Hebrew sign-off for ending phone calls, leaving a cafe, or parting ways on the street: 'יַאלְלָה בַּיי!' (combining Arabic 'yalla' + English 'bye'). Quick, cheerful, and iconic.

letters.name: Alef
letters.clue: An 'X' shape with a diagonal spine. A quiet carrier that takes the sound of any vowel attached to it.

letters.name: Shin
letters.clue: Looks like a crown with 3 horns. A dot on the right top horn says 'sh'!

letters.name: Lamed
letters.clue: The tallest letter in Hebrew, reaching up high like a giraffe neck or flagpole. Sound: 'l'.

letters.name: Mem
letters.clue: Has an open bottom-left corner like an open wave or mouth. Sound: 'm'.

letters.name: Mem Sofit (Final Mem)
letters.clue: A neat closed square box. At the end of a word, Mem turns into this closed square box!

letters.name: Bet
letters.clue: A square house with an open left door and a dot (Dagesh) in its belly: Belly dot = 'b'!

letters.name: Vet
letters.clue: Same shape as Bet, but WITHOUT the belly dot. It makes a soft 'v' sound.

letters.name: Kuf
letters.clue: Looks like a key with a tail hanging below the baseline. Makes a crisp 'k' sound.

letters.name: Pei
letters.clue: Looks like an open mouth with a tooth (the dot). 'P' for pizza with a dot!

letters.name: Fei Sofit (Final Fei)
letters.clue: At the end of a word, Pei uncurls its tail straight down and loses the dot, making a soft 'f' sound.

letters.name: Chet
letters.clue: A solid doorway or arch with an unbroken roof bridge. Makes that famous Israeli throaty 'ch' sound!

letters.name: Resh
letters.clue: A rounded right-angle corner (like a rounded right turn). Gently rolled in the back of the throat.

letters.name: Tav
letters.clue: Has a solid left foot sticking out like a heavy toe. Sound: 't'.

letters.name: Yod
letters.clue: The smallest letter in Hebrew, floating like a little apostrophe near the top. Sound: 'y' or 'ee'.

letters.name: Dalet
letters.clue: Looks like a door frame with a small ledge sticking out at the top-right corner. Sound: 'd'.

letters.name: Kaf
letters.clue: A rounded crescent C-shape with a dot inside. Makes a crisp 'k' sound.

letters.name: Khaf
letters.clue: Same rounded crescent shape as Kaf, but without the dot. Makes the throaty 'ch' sound.

letters.name: Khaf Sofit (Final Khaf)
letters.clue: At the end of a word, Khaf drops its lower bar straight down into a long tail below the baseline.

letters.name: Nun
letters.clue: A narrow hook sitting on a base line. Sound: 'n'.

letters.name: Nun Sofit (Final Nun)
letters.clue: At the end of a word, Nun straightens out into a long vertical line below the baseline.

letters.name: Samech
letters.clue: A completely closed round circle or oval. Pure clean 's' sound.

letters.name: Ayin
letters.clue: Looks like a 'Y' with two branches meeting. Means 'eye' in Hebrew; carries vowels with deep resonance.

letters.name: Tsadi
letters.clue: Looks like an antenna with a little arm. Makes the snappy 'ts' sound.

letters.name: Tsadi Sofit (Final Tsadi)
letters.clue: At the end of a word, Tsadi unrolls its bottom bar into a long tail dropping below the line.

letters.name: Zayin
letters.clue: A slender vertical rod with a crowned hammer cap. Sound: 'z'.

letters.name: He
letters.clue: Looks like a doorway with a gap in the top-left corner. Breath of air 'h'.

letters.name: Vav
letters.clue: A simple vertical nail with a small hook on top. Can sound like 'v', 'o' (וֹ), or 'u' (וּ).

letters.name: Tet
letters.clue: A curved basket or pot curling in from the right. Crisp 't' sound.

letters.name: Sin
letters.clue: The same 3-pronged crown as Shin, but with the dot on the LEFT top horn, giving it a clean 's' sound.
